title: Every Decision Has a Clock
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article argues that the timing of a decision can matter as much as the decision itself, describing every major choice as having a hidden window during which it will have its greatest effect. It lays out the tension leaders must manage between deferring a decision to gather more information and stakeholder input, and acting before the window of opportunity closes. The piece notes that most poor decisions stem from something the leader didn't know, favoring deliberate patience, but insists this should never be confused with indecisiveness once the moment to act arrives.
points: Every major decision carries a hidden window of ideal timing, and poor timing can undercut an otherwise sound choice.
Deliberately deferring a decision allows leaders to gather more data, involve stakeholders, and track market shifts.
The number one cause of poor decisions is information the leader simply didn't know at the time.
Deferring a decision is not the same as indecisiveness — good leaders act vigorously once the moment arrives.
Leaders must watch for signals that the window is closing, including team paralysis waiting on a decision.
quotes: Experienced leaders and decision-makers know that the timing of a decision can be as critical as the choice itself.
Every decision has an ideal window of time from which the advantages of the choice can be fully realized.
The best leaders don’t make a decision until they have to. They prize the optionality inherent in studying a problem and not acting on it until it is necessary.
Not surprisingly, the number one reason leaders make a poor decision is something they didn’t know.
The push and pull of keeping options open while not losing the opportunity to seize the moment is inherent in all good decision-making.
